## Summary

Research confidence is **Moderate**. Some of this break's ideal conditions are confirmed by sources; others rest on limited evidence. It is the class the app computes from the evidence (how well the break's ideal conditions are documented), not a forecast and not a probability.

Main gaps:

- Limited information is available about the wave sizes this break works in.
- Limited information is available about the swell period this break needs.

| Swell size | Low | Supported by one source (a surf magazine) (based on search summaries; source pages not read in full) |
| Swell period | Low | Supported by one source (a forecast site's spot guide). |

Research notes (research_evidence.json):

> Eight sources from eight publishers, six read directly (ScienceDirect and Surfertoday are 403 and kept from the search pass). The page gives 2004 and 230,000 m3 for the dredging, ScienceDirect's summary 2003, and Save The Waves 243,000 m3. Swell direction (NW) agrees everywhere it is stated, but Breakfinder's templated line says NNE. Wind: S (Surf-Forecast), S-SW (Surf Atlas intro, Breakfinder, Surfertoday) agree with the profile's 180; Surf Atlas's spot section says SE, a conflict within that page (recorded at the 45-deg edge). Tide: low (Surf-Forecast, Surf Atlas) to low-mid (Breakfinder, Surfertoday) all overlap the profile's low to mid; a rising tide after low is preferred by Surf Atlas, a falling one by Surf-Forecast. Season: autumn peak (Surf Atlas), winter over 50% surfable (Wikipedia), September-December (Surfertoday); February-March is supported only by Surf Atlas's 'can be in winter or spring'. Sand bottom, dated: dredging in 2003-2004 destroyed the sandbar, and the 2005 contest was cancelled; it began to recover in 2006 (Save The Waves 2008; Wikipedia; npj Ocean Sustainability 2023). No measured surf-zone bathymetry was found. Ride length conflict: 200 m (Surf Atlas) vs 400 m (Save The Waves, Breakfinder). Frequency: 50-70 days a year (Surf Atlas), about 50 (Surfertoday), one day in three 'perfect' (Wikipedia). Breakfinder caution: its header calls Mundaka an A-frame beach break; only its descriptive paragraphs were used. Save The Waves is an NGO-commissioned economic study (community). The npj piece is a short journal comment. Gaps: no swell period figure (only 'groundswell'); size numbers only from Surfertoday (not re-readable, 403).

## Ideal conditions

Directions are compass degrees the swell or wind comes FROM, ranges clockwise. Heights keep the scale each source states (breaking face, Hawaiian, swell or relative to the surfer); the app's sizes are breaking face heights in feet. Sources are numbered as in [Sources](#sources).

### Swell height

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum suitable | — | not documented | — | `wave_height_min_ft` 4 ft (breaking face) |
| Ideal range | 6–10 ft | documented | S4 | no separate setting; working range 4–12 ft |
| Maximum suitable | 12 ft (face) | documented | S4 | `wave_height_max_ft` 12 ft (breaking face) |

Notes:

- **Minimum suitable**: No excerpt gives the size at which the wave starts working.
- **Ideal range**: Surfertoday (search summary, not read directly) says its barrels typically shine in the 6-10 ft range; the sentence implies face height since it continues with faces up to about 12 ft.
  - S4 (Surfertoday): “Its textbook barrels typically shine in the six-to-ten-foot range, though the break can hold faces up to about 12 feet.”
- **Maximum suitable**: Surfertoday (search summary, not read directly) says the break can hold faces up to about 12 ft.
  - S4 (Surfertoday): “Its textbook barrels typically shine in the six-to-ten-foot range, though the break can hold faces up to about 12 feet.”

### Swell direction

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ideal bearing | 315–337.5° (NW to NNW, clockwise) | documented | S2, S4, S5, S8 | `optimal_swell_direction` 310–340° (NW to NNW, clockwise) |
| Acceptable range | — | not documented | — | `swell_window` 290–20° (WNW to NNE, clockwise) |
| Blocked directions | — | not documented | — | no separate setting (outside `swell_window`) |
| Exposure | fairly exposed; NW swell wraps into the bay | documented | S2, S8 | no setting |

Notes:

- **Ideal bearing**: Surf-Forecast, the Surf Atlas and BreakFinder name a northwest swell (BreakFinder: it must wrap into the bay to hit the sandbar at the right angle) and Surfertoday (search summary) names north-northwest.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “the ideal swell angle is from the northwest”
  - S5 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “They're mostly in autumn but can be in winter or spring, and occur when the NW Atlantic groundswells meet a SW offshore wind.”
  - S8 (BreakFinder (breakfinder.surf)): “It requires a strong Northwest (NW) swell to wrap into the bay and hit the sandbar at the correct angle.”
  - S4 (Surfertoday): “The wave comes alive with a north-northwest Atlantic swell paired with offshore south or southwest winds.”
- **Acceptable range**: No excerpt gives an outer swell window.
- **Blocked directions**: No excerpt names blocked directions; Surfertoday only says the wave is highly sensitive to swell angle.
- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it a fairly exposed river break and BreakFinder says the NW swell has to wrap into the bay.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Mundaka in Pais Vasco is a fairly exposed river break that has consistent surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat.”
  - S8 (BreakFinder (breakfinder.surf)): “It requires a strong Northwest (NW) swell to wrap into the bay and hit the sandbar at the correct angle.”

Notes:

- **Preferred stage**: Surf-Forecast and the Surf Atlas say low tide, BreakFinder and Surfertoday (search summary) low to mid, and both of the latter say the wave disappears at high tide.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Best around low tide when the tide is falling.”
  - S5 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “Only good on a low tide that's past the turn”
  - S4 (Surfertoday): “The best time of day is from low to mid-tide, since at high tide the surf lines disappear.”
  - S8 (BreakFinder (breakfinder.surf)): “Mundaka works best from Low to Mid tide. At high tide, the wave often disappears or backs off completely.”
- **Rising or falling**: Surf-Forecast says best around low tide when the tide is falling, whereas the Surf Atlas says it is only good on a low tide that is past the turn.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Best around low tide when the tide is falling.”
  - S5 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “Only good on a low tide that's past the turn”
- **Size-dependent preference**: No excerpt links the tide preference to swell size.
- **Local tide data**: App tide data, not research evidence: data/tide_stations.json links this spot to the EOT20 global tide model cell eot20:mundaka (datum model mean sea level), 11.0 km from the break, as primary (looked in data/tide_stations.json, data/tides/constants_eot20.json and docs/tides.md); the app shows predicted astronomical tides only; catalog caveat: River-mouth break at the Urdaibai estuary; the model cell is in the open Bay of Biscay, so times and heights at the river mouth may differ.

### Seasonality

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prime months | common to all sources: Sep, Oct, Nov; widest stated: Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec | documented | S4, S5 | `best_months` Oct, Nov, Dec, Jan, Feb, Mar |
| Secondary season | winter (sometimes spring); summer mostly flat | documented | S1, S2, S5 | no setting |
| Swell sources | NW Atlantic groundswells | documented | S4, S5 | no setting |
| Wind patterns | regular southerly winds; summer easterlies switch south in autumn | documented | S5 | no setting |

Notes:

- **Prime months**: The Surf Atlas says autumn is the peak, with the NW swell switching on around October, and Surfertoday (search summary) gives September through December as the most cited window.
  - S5 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “Autumn is the peak time for Mundaka. The NW swell channel fires up around October and the summer easterlies switch south.”
  - S4 (Surfertoday): “The most cited window is September through December.”
- **Secondary season**: Wikipedia says the chance of surfing exceeds 50% in winter (62% of January days), the Surf Atlas says good days can also come in winter or spring, and Surf-Forecast says summer tends to be mostly flat.
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “During winter, the possibility of surfing surpasses 50%. In January, 62% of days are surfable.”
  - S5 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “They're mostly in autumn but can be in winter or spring, and occur when the NW Atlantic groundswells meet a SW offshore wind.”
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Mundaka in Pais Vasco is a fairly exposed river break that has consistent surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat.”
- **Swell sources**: The Surf Atlas names NW Atlantic groundswells and Surfertoday (search summary) a north-northwest Atlantic swell.
  - S5 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “They're mostly in autumn but can be in winter or spring, and occur when the NW Atlantic groundswells meet a SW offshore wind.”
  - S4 (Surfertoday): “The wave comes alive with a north-northwest Atlantic swell paired with offshore south or southwest winds.”
- **Wind patterns**: The Surf Atlas says the wave is groomed by regular southerly winds and that the summer easterlies switch south around October.
  - S5 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “Groomed by regular southerly winds...occur when the NW Atlantic groundswells meet a SW offshore wind”
  - S5 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “Autumn is the peak time for Mundaka. The NW swell channel fires up around October and the summer easterlies switch south.”

### Geography

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Break type | rivermouth (left over an estuary sandbar) | documented | S1, S2, S4, S6, S8 | `break_type` rivermouth, `wave_direction` left |
| Orientation | — | not documented | — | nearshore-model shore normal estimated as the centre of the optimal swell direction (325° (NW)) |
| Exposure | fairly exposed | documented | S2 | no setting |
| Bathymetry | triangular estuary sandbar (ebb-tidal delta) built from river silt; destroyed by dredging in 2003-2004 and partly recovered from 2006 | documented | S1, S3, S5, S6, S7 | no measured bathymetry (profile derived from the swell windows) |

Notes:

- **Break type**: Surfertoday (search summary) calls it a left-hander at a river mouth, BreakFinder a left peeling along a triangular sandbar formed by the estuary, Save The Waves a left formed by a sandbar, Wikipedia an estuary sandbar, and Surf-Forecast a river break.
  - S4 (Surfertoday): “Mundaka is a left-hander breaking at a river mouth, and it is highly sensitive to tides, rainfall, and swell and wind angles.”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “The estuary at Mundaka created a perfect sandbar that forms hollow waves.”
  - S8 (BreakFinder (breakfinder.surf)): “this wave peels for up to 400 meters along a triangular sandbar formed by the Urdaibai estuary.”
  - S6 (Save The Waves Coalition): “famous 400 meter long left hand wave naturally formed by a sandbar”
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Mundaka in Pais Vasco is a fairly exposed river break that has consistent surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat.”
- **Orientation**: No excerpt gives the sandbar or coast orientation.
- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it a fairly exposed river break.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Mundaka in Pais Vasco is a fairly exposed river break that has consistent surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat.”
- **Bathymetry**: The Surf Atlas describes a triangular sandbank of river silt and ScienceDirect (search summary) the sandbar as the estuary's ebb delta; ScienceDirect dates the damaging dredging to 2003, Wikipedia and Save The Waves to 2004, npj says the wave was lost in 2005, and Wikipedia and Save The Waves say it came back from 2006, not fully to its original form.
  - S5 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “It's powered by a triangular sandbank that's built-up from silt deposits coming off the river.”
  - S3 (Elsevier (ScienceDirect)): “The ebb delta is formed by the Mundaka sand bar, a worldwide recognized surfing spot, whose morphology is the result of the morphodynamic interactions between the beach, the inlet...”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “The estuary at Mundaka created a perfect sandbar that forms hollow waves.”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “In 2004, more than 230,000 cubic meters of sand was dredged from the Urdaibai estuary...By 2006, conditions had improved to allow the Billabong Pro Mundaka to return”
  - S3 (Elsevier (ScienceDirect)): “the last artificial movements of sand (dredging and dumping) within the estuary, carried out in 2003, altered the natural sedimentary equilibrium at the ebb tidal delta and the associated sandbar”
  - S6 (Save The Waves Coalition): “In 2004 a dredging project was needed to move the latest ship out to sea but an unfortunate side effect of this dredging was the destruction of the sandbar that shapes the wave.”
  - S6 (Save The Waves Coalition): “The wave began to rejuvenate during the summer of 2006 and although not fully back to its original form”
  - S7 (npj Ocean Sustainability (Nature Portfolio)): “In 2005, two European waves were lost due to building and dredging activities in...Mundaka (Basque Country, Spain). While the disappearance of the Mundaka wave was only temporary”

## Conflicting information

- **Wind · offshore**: Surf-Forecast gives south, Surfertoday (search summary) and BreakFinder south or southwest and the Surf Atlas intro southerly/SW, but the Surf Atlas spot section says SE offshore winds are perfect, contradicting its own intro.
- **Tide · rising or falling**: Surf-Forecast says best around low tide when the tide is falling, whereas the Surf Atlas says it is only good on a low tide that is past the turn.
